title: Present simple and regular past
rule: Use the present simple for habits and facts (I walk to school), and add -ed for most past actions (Yesterday I walked).
examples: Every day she plays cricket. | Last week we visited Amma.
tip: Time words help: every day → present; yesterday, last week → past.
check_question: Choose the right verb: Yesterday we ___ to the park.
check_options: A. walk | B. walked | C. walks
check_explanation: Yesterday tells you it is the past: walked.

title: Common irregular past forms
rule: Many common verbs do not take -ed in the past: go → went, buy → bought, see → saw, eat → ate.
examples: We went to the market and bought mangoes. | I saw a film and ate popcorn.
tip: Learn these by heart; never write goed or buyed.
check_question: Choose the right verb: She ___ a new bag last week.
check_options: A. buyed | B. bought | C. buy

title: Questions and negatives with did
rule: After did and didn't, use the base form of the verb: Did you go? I didn't see it. (Not: Did you went?)
examples: Did she finish her homework? | We didn't watch TV.
tip: did already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form.
check_options: A. saw | B. see | C. seen
check_explanation: After did, use the base form: see.

title: Keeping the tense steady
rule: When you tell a story in the past, keep it in the past: She opened the door and saw a dog. Learn less common irregular forms: catch → caught, choose → chose, lead → led.
examples: He caught the ball and threw it back. | They chose a leader who led them well.
tip: Read your sentences again and check every verb is in the same time.
check_question: Choose: The team ___ the cup last year.
check_options: A. win | B. won | C. wins
check_explanation: last year is the past: won.

title: Uncommon irregular forms
rule: Some irregular verbs are rare but appear in books: seek → sought, weep → wept, forbid → forbade, bear → bore.
examples: They sought help from the teacher. | She wept with joy.
tip: If you are unsure, check a dictionary: it lists irregular past forms.

title: He, she, it + -s
rule: In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb after he, she, it or one person or thing: she sings, he fixes, the dog barks.
examples: My aunt teaches music. | It rains a lot in July.
tip: I, you, we, they: no -s (they play).

title: Plural subjects
rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb: the mice run, the trees grow, my cousins live nearby.
examples: The birds are on the roof. | These shoes look new.
tip: Find the subject first, then match the verb to it.

title: Two subjects with and
rule: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Anil and Sara are friends.
examples: My sister and I walk to school. | Bread and butter is…
tip: and adds the subjects together, so the verb is plural.

title: Words between subject and verb
rule: The verb agrees with the subject, not with a noun just before it: The jar of sweets is empty. The cup of tea is hot.
examples: The colour of the flowers is bright. | The boys in the team are tired.
tip: Cover the words between: 'The box … is'.

check_explanation: The subject is the basket (one): is.

title: Each, every, everyone
rule: each, every, everyone, nobody and somebody take a singular verb: Each of the girls has a ticket. Everyone is here.
examples: Every child needs sleep. | Somebody is at the door.
tip: Each of the… is still one at a time: singular.

title: either … or, neither … nor
rule: With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt. Either the girls or their father is coming.
examples: Either my parents or my aunt is coming. | Neither the dog nor the cats were hungry.
tip: Look at the subject closest to the verb.
check_question: Choose: Neither Priya nor her brothers ___ at home.
check_explanation: The nearer subject, brothers, is plural: are.

title: Inverted order; a number of
rule: When the verb comes first, find the subject after it: There are many birds. Here comes the bus. 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular.
examples: A number of shops were closed. | The number of cars is growing.
tip: Turn the sentence round: many birds are there.

title: a or an
rule: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and a before a consonant: an orange, an egg, a ball, a cat.
examples: an inkpot, an onion | a pencil, a dog
tip: Say it aloud: 'an apple' is easier to say than 'a apple'.

title: a first, then the
rule: Use a when you first mention something, then the when you mention it again: I found a shell. The shell was pink. Use a before a job: He is a farmer.
examples: We bought a kite. The kite was red. | My uncle is a doctor.
tip: a = one of many; the = the one we both know about.

title: a or an by sound

examples: an honour | a uniform, a European city

title: the for one of a kind
rule: Use the for things there is only one of, or that everyone knows: the moon, the sky, the Prime Minister.
examples: The sky is clear today. | Close the door, please.
tip: If there is only one, it is the.

title: No a with uncountable nouns
rule: Some nouns cannot be counted: luggage, bread, water, news, rice. Do not use a or an with them: some luggage, a piece of bread.
examples: We bought some bread. | There is a lot of traffic today.
tip: If you cannot put a number in front of it, do not use a or an.

title: General statements
rule: For general statements about all of something, use no article with plurals and abstract nouns: Elephants are strong. Kindness is important.
examples: Dogs are loyal. | Patience is useful.
tip: Talking about all of them, in general? No article.

title: Articles with names
rule: Most names of people, cities and countries have no article (Delhi, India), but rivers, oceans and some countries do: the Yamuna, the Indian Ocean, the United States. Mountains do not: Mount Abu.
examples: We sailed on the Yamuna. | We visited Mount Abu.
